speechtext:
There is one important point which requires consideration. If any one looks over the casualty lists of the Canadian forces, especially those of the spring and early summer, he will find that in a great many cases the next of kin of the men who went from Canada, and who were killed, were residents of the British Isles, so that the pensions we pay will go to people who live in Great Britain, to the children, widows, or mothers, as the case may be. That is going to give rise to this state of affairs, that the next of kin of the soldiers who have gone to fight from Canada and who have been killed, living in Great Britain will get pensions very considerably . higher than those paid to the next of kin of British soldiers who live in Canada or Great Britain. I think that is a matter worthy of some consideration.
The new scheme of pensions was drawn up by a committee of the Militia Council in consultation with a subcommittee of the Privy Council who had before them the scales of pensions paid in other countries. The pensions for totally disabled soldiers are based, to a very large extent, on those introduced by the Parliament of Australia. In the case of totally disabled soldiers, it will be noted that the Canadian rates are slightly higher than the Australian rates, and considerably higher than the British rates. In the United States there are a number of rates for different classes of disability, and these are awarded without any regard to the rank of the individual, with the consequent result that the rates for disability of soldiers is much higher than in any other country; but it should be noted that special provision exists in the Canadian scale by which the pension may be increased by one-third if the soldier requires the constant services of an attendant.
As regards officers-in the case of those who are single-my summing up is that the Canadian rates are -higher than the Australian rates, but considerably lower than the British rates. The Canadian rates for the widows-of soldiers are almost exactly the same -as those recently provided in the Australian Act, and they are practically double the amounts authorized for the widows of British soldiers, although in Great Britain the rates have been materially increased since the outbreak of waT. The rates allowed to widows of soldiers of the United States -are considerably lower than the Canadian rates. As regards officers the Canadian rates for
widows of lieutenants -and captains are almost exactly the -same in Canada, Australia, -and Great Britain, with the advantage slightly in favour of Canada. As regards officers of -higher rank, majors and lieutenant-colonels, the Canadian rates are higher than the Australian, hut l-ess than the British. In both Canada an-d Great Britain on the widow re-marrying, a gratuity equivalent to two years pension is granted on re-marriage taking place.^ The only other point worth mentioning is that in Great Britain an increase o-f pension of $30 a year is given to a soldier's widow on attaining the age of 35 years, and another increase of $30 on attaining the age of 45 years, but even with this increase the rates do not come up to the Canadian rates.
This, as I said, is a proper -subject for discussion in the House, -and the Government will welcome the discussion of it and any suggestions that may be made. * I do not think there is a m-an in this House who would attempt to make political capital out of the question of pensions. We are all striving to provide a -pension rate that will be fair to the brave men who are going forward to the front to fight the battles of Canada and of the Empire.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps you will permit me to transgress a little -and prolong my remarks beyond six o'clock. There are one or two other -matters with which I would like to deal, an-d I think my remarks would come sooner to an end if I were -allowed to continue before the adjournment for dinner. My bon. friend the -member for St. Jo-hn (Mr. Pugsley) made certain references to the extension of the term of Parliament. My hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) -also referred to it. He h-a-s always been a -stout upholder of the Constitution of this country, -and I -have always respected his opinions on matters of this sort, for I know him to be sincere. He pratically t-ol-d us he -had an open mind on the subject and that although he was always prepared to stand behind the Constitution he might vote in favour of an extension. My hon. friend from St. John, however, has discovered that the question is -a most serious one, that we have to interfere with the British North America Act, and th-at that i-s -a -most serious thing to contemplate. Ye-t, it is no more s-eriou-s now than it was on 15th September last, and on the 15th day of September last my hon. friend from St. John knew as well as when he delivered his speech on the Address that, if there was to he an extension

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
of the term of Parliament, there would have to be an amendment to the British North America Act, because without legislation by the Imperial Parliament this Parliament has not the -power to extend its term. I find that on the 15th September last my hon. friend from St. John, in the city of Winnipeg, declared to a reporter of the Free Press:
The present circumstances are so grave from the standpoint of Canada and the Empire that it would be deplorable in my opinion to have the people divided upon party questions. -
Another of the reasons why X favour putting off an election until after the war is because X think it would be a great pity to hold one just when the energies of all the people of Canada, and especially the members of the Government who are primarily charged with the duty of attending to the recruiting and equipment of the soldiers should be devoted to this one end.
Why this sudden change? Why is he so impressed with the importance of the matter now when he was not so impressed with it in September. It may be due to the - fact that in September last the Government was supposed to be contemplating an election, and my hon. friend thought he would put himself 'squarely against such a proposal as something opposed to the best interests of the country. But now, when the Government comes to Parliament and asks for an extension of the term, my hon. friend must again be against the Government -and so he is deeply impressed with the importance of the question, an importance which ihe did not see in September when -he was interviewed by the Winnipeg Free Press.
But my hon. friend from St. John was not alone in making such -a statement. My hon. friend from Bed Deer (Mr. Clark) whose criticisms, -as I said before, are always moderate, and none -the less effective because of their moderation, also placed himself squarely on record as opposed to an election during the period of the war. Then my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) -has practically -said the same thing in speeches he has made and in interviews he has had throughout the country. I might refer to the -address he gave in the House of Commons on 19th of August when he said:
Speaking for those who sit around me, speaking for the wide constituencies which we represent in this House, I hasten to say that to ail these measures we are prepared to give immediate assent. If in what has been done or in what remains to be done there may be anything which in our judgment should not he done or should be differently done, we raise

no question, we take no exception, we offer no criticism and we shall offer no criticism so long as there is danger at the front.
Then the righ-t hon. gentleman in a speech delivered at the Montreal Beform Club on December 12, 1914, declared that:
As soon as war was declared we thought it was part of the duty we owed, not only to our policy, but also to our country, to lay down for the time being, all party discussion, and to give our whole thought and energy to the new problems which were brought by the war, and not in any way embarrass the Government, but on the contrary to facilitate its duty which this new situation created for the Government.
At the present time the only thing we have to think of is to finish the war, and to adjourn to a future date those domestic problems which will have to be taken up later.
The war is still on. Upon the policy introduced by the Government to discharge the duties we owe to the Mother Country, we have taken no issue with the Government. We have supported their policy, and therefore there is no cause for an appeal to the country.
I am as strong a party man as there is in Canada, but at the present time I overlook all my connection as a party man, simply to remember the duty which I owe to the Mother Country, England, and I must add to France also, the land of my ancestors.
The hon. member for Pietou, N.S., (Mr. Macdonald) was interviewed by the Toronto Star on September 17, on which occasion he made this statement:
An election while the struggle is raging for liberty and humanity would be a crime. An election during the war would divide the Dominion ; there should be no election during the war.
The Toronto Globe on September 6, 1915, said:
If the war is still in progress.... Liberals will be just as keen to postpone a general election as Conservatives. Election talk should cease. It distracts attention from the greatest work Canadian statesmen and the Canadian people have had to do since Confederation.
On October 20 the Toronto Globe said:
, To secure an absolute insurance against partisan strife in our national political arena there must be an agreement for the extension of the Parliamentary term until a period some time after the close of the war.
The Toronto Star, on September 9, said:
We do not want an election now, or during the war.
The Star again says:
As there is a general agreement of opinion that there should be no election during the war there should he no difficulty in making the arrangement referred to (extension of parliamentary term). It would be an advantage, not only to have the election deferred until after the war, but to put an end to the nuisance of periodical election rumors.

The Winnipeg Free Press of August 23, 1915:
A bitter party election in Canada would be a deplorable diversion of national energy.
The Chronicle, Halifax, April 12, 1915:
We need not pause to remark that election day should not come until the war is over. Every decent-minded Canadian, regardless of party, knows and admits that.
In the Chronicle of September 13 and also of September 16 a similar opinion is expressed. The Recorder, Brockville, says:
Both parties in Great Britain have agreed that there will be no election until after the war is over. From Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and every other outlying part of the Empire come similar announcements. Canada alone talks of a party conflict at a time when [DOT] none should be for party, but all be for the state.' This country would present a fine spectacle to the Empire, and to the rest of the world, if an acrimonious conflict should held while the Empire is fighting for its very existence.
The Herald of Montreal, in December last, put the case against an election very strongly and the Free Press, Ottawa, on May'll, said that at the next session Sir Robert Borden should introduce enabling legislation extending the life of Parliament. The Ottawa Citizen on April 14, said that it did not believe that the people of either party wish a general election and the Times of St. John, N.B., the particular supporter of my hon. friend from St. John, says:
All that Sir Robert Borden needs to do is to announce that there will be no election until after the war.
Yet, in spite of his own previous declarations, in spite of all these pronouncements by prominent men in the Liberal party and their leading journals, my hon. friend has discovered that it is a very serious thing to taut about amending the British North America Act so as to provide for the extension of the parliamentary term.
The hon. member for Richmond, N.S., (Mr. Kyte) spoke the other night about the evidences of patronage in connection with shell matters in Cape Breton and more particularly in connection with the appointment of inspectors. My hon. friend stated that nobody could be appointed as an inspector unless he had a recommendation from the Borden Club or some other political organization there. I am not quoting my hon. friend's exact words but that was the effect of them. What are the facts, as I am informed? I am informed that the chief inspector of the district of Cane Breton is Mr. A. E. Strubel, whose appointment did not come through the Borden Club, or any Conservative candidate, or any political pull of any kind whatsoever. He had been the chief inspector for the Canadian Inspection Bureau, which is the bureau that inspected shells that were manufactured under the direction of the Shell Committee, or of the Imperial Munitions Board. He had been chief inspector for the Canadian ' Inspection Bureau before the Government inspection service wa3 organized and he continued the work under the new arrangement. 1 am informed by my correspondent that he does not believe that there are a dozen persons on either side of politics in Cape Breton county who know on what side of politics Mr. Strubel is, and as far as anybody knows he has never yet cast a vote in a Dominion or provincial election in this country. The inspector who stands next to Mr. Strubel, I am informed, in the matter of salary received, is Mr. D. E. Ross, a Liberal in politics, secretary of the Sydney Fielding Club, and son of Mr. A. C. Ross, formerly the Liberal member for Cape Breton North and Victoria. Another inspector is Mr. Wells Woodill, who is a Liberal, whose father was a Liberal, and all of whose brothers and immediate relatives belong to the Liberal party. For the appointments which have been made during the past six months, I am told, Mr. Strubel gives the assurance that he himself is personally responsible. Naturally he has received letters of solicitation from politicians, but he has never been influenced by them. Some time ago he wrote to a gentleman who had urged an appointment for political reasons, advising him that all appointments would be made on merit, and that preference would be given to Canadian wounded soldiers who had returned from the front. I am told that there are at present six inspectors under Mr. Strubel, three Liberals and three Conservatives. Mr. Strubel, I am informed, is not in any sense a political partisan or connected with any political organization in any way. The statements made by my hon. friend from Richmond are wide of the mark, and he must have received inaccurate information in regard to the matter.
Who is my hon. friend's authority?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not the right to give the authority now, but I will see if I may be permitted to do it.

I might suggest to my hon. friend that if any question be raised as to why Mr. Ross had received his

appointment, the answer would be that it was because his father had renounced the religion of his fathers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know anything about that. I am simply giving the House the information I have received.

I am giving my hon.
friend the correct information.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not know Mr. Ross, but I come to the conclusion, from the hon. gentleman's remarks, that Mr. Ross must be a very sensible man. I must trespass no further upon the time of the
6 p.m. House, which I have already occupied too long. When I addressed the Canadian Club at Boston a few months ago, I pointed out that after the war is over there will, no doubt, come a period of reconstruction for Canada, as for all the other countries engaged in the conflict, which will be followed, I believe, by an era of tremendous expansion, so far as our Dominion is concerned, caused by an immense influx of population, attracted to our country by its fertile lands, its moderate taxes, its democratic institutions, and the opportunities which it affords to every man within its borders of acquiring for himself a happy home, and of winning position and distinction if his talents and character entitle him to do so. We have no doubt in Canada of what the ultimate result of the war will be. While no man can foretell its duration, we conscientiously believe that our cause is just, and that there is an unflinching determination to make it triumphant. In the language of Sir Robert Borden, any reverses that have come or may come in the future will only inspire us with deeper courage and a greater determination.
All that our fathers fought for and achieved, all that we have inherited and accomplished, our institutions, our liberties, our destiny as a nation, the existence of our Empire, are all at stake in this contest, and we are confident that the resolution, the determination, the self-reliance, and the resourcefulness that have never failed Canada irr the stress and trials of the past will assuredly not fail her now.
Since Parliament prorogued in April last we have had some disappointments, and events have not moved so rapidly and favourably as we then believed they would, but the spirit of the Allies of Canada and of the Empire is undiminished, and there is an even greater and more serious determination than existed months ago to bring

the war to a successful close. Recruiting in Canada has proceeded satisfactorily, and in Great Britain political difficulties that at one time seemed threatening and serious have largely disappeared. No matter how long the war may last, or how serious the sacrifices, personal and national, that must be made, and which Canadians, in common with the inhabitants of other portions of the Empire, are fully prepared to undergo, we will always remember that:
Freedom's battle once begun,
Bequeathed from bleeding sire to son, Though baffled oft, is ever won.
It is freedom's battle that is now being waged, and the Canadians in the battle line are fighting for freedom's sacred cause.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, this is the sixth session of this Parliament and the third session since the v war began, and I think it might not be out of place, in speaking to the Address in this third war session to recall briefly the changing events, so far as Parliament is concerned, since August 1914. We all remember that, like a bolt from the blue, the news of conflict came, and the representatives' of Canada in Parliament, called suddenly together, came here to take counsel as to what our attitude was to be in a war, the extent and consequence of which we had then but little knowledge. With one accord, disregarding party lines and previous political disputes this Parliament voted to give all that was necessary in the way of money, and of men in the field to help the Empire. There came a period of doubt and suspense when throughout this land as well as throughout the whole of the English-speaking world, there were discussions as to the effect of this White Paper, and that Yellow Paper, and as to which nation was responsible for the initiation of the war. These discussions, without any marked event, attracted a great deal of attention until we met about one year ago. And even then,
I think it will be conceded, that honourable members of this House as a body were not impressed with the deep consequences of this mighty struggle.
We came through that session with a shadow overhanging us, yet we were not given up wholly and exclusively to the contemplation of what our duties and our rights were in the circumstances. Honourable gentlemen on the other side of the House claimed our attention for some time

with what I think will be recognized to-day to have been a rather singular measure in view of the peculiar world situation, a proposition that we should send to Flanders- [DOT]and, as it would appear now, to the Dardanelles also-ito take the votes of the boys who had gone out to fight for liberty. That proposition	was	seriously discussed one year ago.	In the light
of events since then, I think it will be conceded that that proposal and that discussion seem very singular indeed. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) told us that the country was demanding in thunder tones some remedy for the alleged evils arising from the decisions of the other branch of this Parliament. I do not believe that the people weie demanding this in .any kind of tones, to say nothing of thunder tones; but I cite these facts to establish the truth of what I say, that we in Parliament last year hardly realized the position in which' the whole world and our own nation stood in relation to this great conflict.
Since that time there has 'been, I am sure every one will concede, a great and marvellous change not only in the feelings of the majority of members of this House but in the feelings and sentiments of the whole Canadian people. We had hardly reached our homes when we were shocked by the news that the German nation had violated every rule of the code which is supposed to guide the relations of belligerents and had sent to the bottom of the ocean hundreds of people in the steamer Lusitania. Then came the woid of the disaster at St. Julien and LangemaTck, when the Canadian boys for the first time felt the stress of conflict, and which cast a shadow of sorrow upon many a home in this land. Then came the after results, the splendid position maintained by our sons at Ypres, where, it is now conceded not only by Canadians but by the sons of Empire everywhere, the bravery, intellli-gence and capacity of our Canadian boys prevented the Germans from coming through to Calais. In the intervening days there has been this stTange, peculiar association of Germany with the Balkan principalities and Turkey, the outcome of the immense ambition of this man who rules the German nation, this personality actuated by the lust for world-wide power, bringing home to us the dangers and seriousness of this war in a measure in which they had never come to us before. Hence it was that from all portions of this land
our boys have gone forth to the conflict, animated with the highest ideals. Here in this House there are vacant chairs of members who have gone to the conflict, while all around us are men whose sons are at the front or are preparing to go at the earliest opportunity. And into the homes of many of our people has come the sorrow for the one who will never return, and there are returning to us the maimed and the blind whom it will he our duty to maintain and provide for in the future.
So, we have met this year under conditions different from any that have characterized the opening of any session of Parliament in the history of our country and,
I believe, under a deeper sense of our duty than we have ever had before. I think the majority of us are animated with the desire in our deliberations to correct the mistakes of the past and to correct them in the full light of day. If this is done it should not call forth complaint or criticism from those who may be responsible for those mistakes. I believe that we desire to provide those things and take those steps which our duty calls for, and, so far as we can look into the future and provide not only for the soldier boys who shall return, but also for the people who shall live in this country happy and prosperous .under the benign rule of the great nation to which we belong. Looking over the history of the year, we, the representatives of a free people, may express ourselves in an adaptation of Lincoln's immortal words: "That we here highly resolve that these dead shall not have died in vain, that, under God, this nation shall have a new birth of freedom, and that government of the people, for the people, and by the people shall not perish from the earth."
With these feelings I approach the consideration of the questions that come before us as representatives of a free people at this time. And I say again, that* if there have beqn mistakes in the past, let us frankly ascertain and correct them; if there are abuses, let them be righted, and let us prepare with all sincerity for our future.	.
Shortly before the New Year the Prime Minister announced that, in addition to the 250,000 men who have already been called to the colours, 250,000 men are to be called and' are to form a quota of Canada's contribution. Let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, that according to the census returns oi 1911 there are, or were at that time, only 1,537,581 men in Canada between the ages

of 20 and 45. That means that if we are to get the 500,000 men, we must take one man out of every three. Without conscription you can get those men only by living up to the highest ideals; you can get them only by impressing them with the fact that the consequences of this conflict are so great that this Government and this Parliament are willing to throw aside the considerations which in the past have furnished ground for complaint and for proper investigation, on the part not only of the Opposition, but also of Parliament as a whole and of the people at large. If hon. gentlemen opposite fall short of this ideal; if they are not guided in every respect by the highest motives, how can they expect one man out of every three in this country to come forward and fight? They need not expect them; they will not come.
The other day the Solicitor General, referring to the hon. member for St. John city, said that he " isolated " him from the other members of the House. Language of that kind from any member of the Government is entirely out of place. If the freedom for which our boys are going out to fight and to die is a really valuable thing, then here where we have freedom we must maintain it. And if hon. gentlemen, speaking as representatives of the free people of this country in the debate, on the Address- where they get an opportunity of pointing out their grievances and asking for redress -aTe to be told that they shall be isolated because they give expression to that which is heard on the streets, read in our newspapers, spoken by supporters of the Government; if, I say, they are to be told that they shall be isolated, I for one protest most emphatically.
I noticed in the Conservative papers that the hon. Solicitor General was stated to have referred to the remarks of the hon. member for St. John City as being along the line, of treachery. I find on looking at Hansard that the Solicitor General did not go that far, and that his remarks were misinterpreted by the press. But the hon. Solicitor General must not be so sensitive of criticism. If this Government will conduct the affairs of the country fairly and honestly, along proper lines, and with the highest ideals in view, they will receive from the Opposition the utmost possible consideration at this time. If, on the other hand, they disregard these ideals; if they sink to lower levels; if they are guilty of mistakes or acts of malfeasance, they may expect criticism; they 
will receive it, and have no right to complain because of it. No government in any British country has a right to set itself up as a body which ought not to be criticised. Just as we object to the domination of the German autocracy, so do we object to the Government's declaring itself to be above the people. We want no kaisers in this country; we want no field marshalls and no crown princes to say that .hon. gentlemen on this side are guilty of lese, majeste if they criticise the Government. Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House realize to the full the tremendous importance to the Empire of the present situation. Let hon. gentlemen on the other side, many of whom realize the seriousness of the situation to the fullest extent, remember that they are the representatives of a democracy, and that that democracy must have its fullest expression in this Parliament, as it should in every other parliament over which the British flag flies.
My hon. friends opposite complain of criticism. Let me suggest to them a very ready way of relieving themselves of a great deal of criticism. Let them abolish the patronage system in the Militia Department in regard to war expenditures; for it is the case that only a Conservative can sell supplies to the Militia Department. The people of this country will find their ideals rudely shattered if that continues to be the practice of hon. gentlemen opposite. After all, a time will come when these men who have the patronage will not be able to expect from other men, actuated by the highest ideals, the highest form of sacrifice in this war. My hon. friends, who are so very sensitive to criticism, can settle that difficulty by simply declaring that they will do as is done in Great Britain; that they will tell the party heelers and the men who want to control the distribution of favours in this, that, or the other constituency, that the nation is in too serious a position for them to potter with dealings of (that kind. Let hon. gentlemen opposite take this opportunity of doing away with that system for ever in Canada. My hon. friends maintain a list in the Militia Department. If, as is the case in my county, no medical man who is not a Tory doctor may examine a recruit who desires to go to the war, I want to know what kind of idealism you are going to have from the Liberal doctors in that and the other Liberal constituencies in Canada.

Why is it that my
hon. friend, who is supposed to be a major in the medical corps, is not down earning his money in Nova Scotia and attending to his business? I want to tell him that I know more about the county of Pictou than he does. I want to tell him that I can give him an instance where men who were supposed by Conservative medical men to be not satisfactory to the gentleman who has the patronage in my constituency were prevented from . examining and reporting upon recruits who wanted to go to the war; that the reports were not received, and that the applicants were compelled to go to a man who was named by the man who had the patronage. My hon. friend, who is a major in the army medical corps in Nova Scotia, should correct that abuse. There is no reason why any duly authenticated medical practitioner in this country, no matter what his politics may be, should not, at first hand, be permitted to certify as to the physical qualifications of the men who want to go and fight. I mention that merely to indicate to my hon. friends that I make this statement on my responsibility as a member of the House, knowing the circumstances as they exist in my county- and having a son who is preparing to go to the front. Will it be said-it is just as well to be clear on this point-that anyone was guilty of treachery or lese majeste last winter when we discussed the question as to _ the wisdom of taking $75,000 out of the Militia Department and giving it to Mr. Foster of Kings to spend in buying horses. Was it improper that that matter should have been investigated? My hon. friend the Minister of Finance should see to it that no department of this Government permits seventy-five thousand dollars or seventy-five thousand cents to be paid out in the way in which that $75,000 was paid out.
The fact that $75,000 can 'be taken out of the treasury of a department of this Government and given to any man to spend carte blanche is not sound and proper administration and the Minister of Finance knows it.
That brings me to the consideration of the matter which was brought up by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). And let me say that the intimation which has been made by some hon. gentlemen opposite as to that hon.. gentleman occupying a position of isolation on this side of
the House is entirely beside the mark. When you find a paper that is ai consistent supporter of the Government, like the Montreal Star, asking an investigation, when you find the Montreal Daily Mail asking for an investigation; when you find this question of shells discussed all over this country in the papers, why should an honourable gentleman be declared to be in an isolated position because, as a representative of the free people, at a time when, under the constitution, these things should be brought to the attention of Parliament, he does so? Does he commit any wrong in doing so? These things are a matter of public notoriety, they are known to the press, they are discussed in all the business centres of Canada. Hon. gentlemen know that. The Government come here and, through their Solicitor General and .their Minister of Marine and Fisheries, absolutely decline to take any position by way of'defence of the Shell 'Committee. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries said this afternoon: I hold no brief for the Shell Committee. The Solicitor General said: I do not stand here as a sponsor for, or as one responsible for the 'conduct of the Shell Committee. I am not here to defend the Shell Committee. I am here to offer some remarks in regard to what they have done, in regard to their status and character, in regard to their responsibility, in regard to our duties [DOT] towards them. But when my hon. friend says further, as he does:
I am not saying and I do not wish to be taken as saying that there cannot he any attack made on the Committee. The Committee may be open to criticism. Nor will I say, under proper authority and at the proper time, there should not be review ot the work of that Committee.
That is the position taken by the Solicitor General. The Minister of Marine says: 1 hold no brief for this committee. He will not undertake the responsibility of defending them. But while he and the Solicitor General take that position and say: We are not responsible for the Shell Committee at all; yet they are able, in some mysterious way, to get from this committee, which they say is connected with the Imperial authorities only, the information which the minister was able to bring to the House this afternoon. It is a very strange committee this, if it is a body having relation entirely with the Imperial Government, for which this Government has no responsibility whatever, if ministers of the Crown here, who wash their hands clear of it, can go and get this information and bring it

down as they did to-day. The position of the Solicitor General in regard to the Shell Committee is very much the position of the lawyer who goes into court and says: I am going to demur to the plaintiff's statement of claim, not upon the ground that it does not disclose good cause of action, not upon tlte ground that it is untrue in any way, and I say the court in which he has brought suit is not the proper court; he should go to some other court. That is the position of the Solicitor General when it is simmered down. Or it might be compared to another position sometimes adopted in court. He confesses the case, but he pleads in avoidance, as we say: It is true that this committee should be investigated, there is no doubt about that, and some time in the future we or somebody else may investigate it, but the man who ventures to stand up in Parliament to-day and say anythiiig about it, is isolated from his friends and from the House, because he ventures to bring to the attention of Parliament this very thing which we say ought to form a matter of investigation.
I want to say in regard to the hon. member for St. John that there are few men in this House, apart from our revered leader, whom we hold in higher esteem. He is a man whom we regard as a great parliamentarian, a man of great ability, as he has demonstrated in this House over and over again, and he has the confidence of every one of us.
No other hon. gentleman in this House but the Solicitor General, with his casuistry, would venture to dispute the soundness of the doctrine which has come down from the days of the revolution, so far as constitutional principles are concerned, that wherever Parliament or the country, for which Parliament stands, or of which it is a representative under British institutions, has had anything to do, directly or indirectly with the spending of money, the expenditure of that money is a proper matter for investigation by Parliament. I stand for that proposition, and I take the statement of the Minister of Finance who told us the other day-and as he indicated in Toronto in his speech before the Board of Trade that Canada was arranging for credits for Great Britain, more particularly with reference to munitions. They have told us that Canada is going to pay for these things, both munitions and other things that are going over to the other side. Yet the Solicitor General comes in and says: It is true that the Shell Committee 
requires to be investigated; I will not defend them for a moment; it is true that they were changed and in some mysterious way a new body called the Imperial Munitions Board came into existence; it is true that we threw them down and all that, yet if anybody wants to make a charge against any Minister of the Crown, we will investigate that, but we will not allow an investigation of the Shell Committee. I assume the papers are going to be brought down. I say that in this Parliament every gentleman should he actuated -by the highest ideals, and if this Government refuse to go on and look into this whole matter in this Parliament, they will be falling short of the ideals they are holding up to the boys of this land whom they are asking to go out and fight 'for liberty. Let us see where we are on this question. It is well to understand it fully, because these issues are apt to be beclouded. We had the story given to us last year by the Prime Minister in regard to the Shell Committee. He told us how it was constituted. It was constituted by the Minister of Militia.
On the 8th of September, 1914, at a meeting held by the minister at the Dominion Arsenal the following Committee was appointed to organize the work throughout the Dominion.
And he gives the names:
About two weeks after the organization of the Committee Mr. Carnegie of London, England, was appointed by the minister as ordnance advisor of the Shell Committee.
He goes on to tell what they did:
The executive work of the committee has been very wisely entrusted to the chairman, Colonel Bertram-[DOT]
The strange part is that this statement is signed by Col. Bertram, in which he states that the executive work has been very widely entrusted to him.
[DOT]-who reports weekly to the Minister of Militia and also to the committee when it meets, which is usually monthly, or more often at the call of the minister.
At this point, I should like to correct my hon. friend the Solicitor General, who I am sorry to see is not here, in regard to the statement he made about the Minister of Militia -and Defence in connection with this committee. "Why," says the Solicitor General in that positive way which he assumes, "the Minister of Militia was present at this Shell Committee only twice, once when it was going out of office and once when the new committee came in;" whereas Col. Bertram says here that when

this committee was appointed all the executitve work was entrusted to the chair- 1 man who reported weekly to the Minister of Mil'itia, and also to the committee which met once a month, or more often at the call of the minister. As I shall show as I go along, the Minister of Militia must have been in close touch with the committee at every stage of its operations; it is so stated here. Who passed -the bills after all? The chartered accountant of the department, says Ool. Bertram:
A chartered accountant recommended by the general manager of the Bank of Montreal, checks the accounts of the committee every month. These are then forwarded to Mr. J. W. Borden, chief accountant for the Militia Department.
Now, why were these accounts forwarded to Mr. J. W. Borden, the Accountant of the Department of Militia? What bad he to do with them? "Why," says the Solicitor General, "we divorced ourselves from this committee," or ratheT he says, "we divorced the committee from us,"-a curious kind of transfer which I think was hardly legal. "We divorced the Shell Committee from the Canadian Government in the matter of responsibility," says the Solicitor General; "we made it a committee under Imperial authority." I would like to know the date when this wonderful divorce took place'.
Mr MURPHY.: After they were fouhd out.

There never was any divorce; there could not be any divorce. It was not a case of "whom God hath joined together let no man put asunder." It was a case of a father disowning his own child. That was the trouble; there could be no question of divorce.
