My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works did not catch what I said. I said it was not a case of marriage or of divorce; it was the case of a father trying to disown bis own child. It was a case of leaving the baby on somebody else's doorstep. Now, I assume that the Government will bring down these orders in council, and 'tell us all about this thing. This is the proposition seriously put forward by a responsible Minister of the Crown; that this Government could call into 'being a committee having the powers which they had in regard to
performing the wonderful duties set out by Col. Bertram in his report, which was read by the Prime Minister last year, and that on their own volition they proceeded to make that creation of theirs a committee under Imperial authority. Well, this Government has done some pretty queer things, but they could not do that, and they have not done it; there is no way in which they 'could do it.
Let us go on and see what Col. Bertram says. These hills were all made out and sent to the Accountant of the Department of Militia.
The Minister of Militia called a meeting of the committee at Ottawa and, after discussing the matter, cabled to Lord Kitchener, pointing out that much larger contracts could be undertaken by the manufacturers of Canada.
Now, I think the 'Solicitor General will be bound to admit that he is wrong in regard to the Minister of Militia being present at only two .meetings, for already we have seen that he was present at three or four. Col. Bertram goes on:
It was proposed by several of the manufacturers that a deputation from the committee should he sent to the War Office, London, to put their claims before the Secretary of State for War. The Minister of Militia dedided on the recommendation of the committee, to send Mr. David Carnegie, as he was familiar with the whole situation.
Is that not a very strange thing, that this body, constituted by the Government, divorced in some mysterious way from the Government, that this body, having been in 'existence for quite a period of time, should -send Mr. Carnegie over to England to tell the Imperial authorities what they could do, or what they could not do. When did this transfer from the Canadian Government to the Imperial Government take place? He goes on to say:
He also informed the various officials at the War Offioe that it was the intention of the Minister of Militia and his committee,, to make ultimately the copper hands in Canada.
So we have this situation: we have this committee constituted by the Minister of Militia, we see that the accounts went to the man who passes the accounts of the Militia Department; and there is no evidence at this moment that in any order in council any powers were given to this body as an imperial institution; on the contrary the evidence shows it has always been a Canadian institution operated by the Minister of Militia as a side wind of his department.
I do not wish to go into detail with regard to the various matters that might

be urged and have been urged from time to time in regard to the Shell Committee; but coming, as I do, from a constituency where, I think, the first shells made in Canada were made by the Nova Scotia Steel Company, I have followed this matter very closely. Colonel Bertram and Mr. Carnegie are the gentlemen who seem to have .been running this committee in regard to the allotment of contracts, and when it is said that there was no politics in the inspection of-shells-I do not care how many letters my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) may read from people in Sydney-if my hon. friend goes to my constituency, he will learn what everybody in the community knows, what my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) who lives in my constituency, knows, something in regard to the carrying on of the industry. We have two systems of inspections in regard to shell construction. There is an inspection which is carried on by the Canadian Inspection Company of Montreal, the inspectors being experts whose business and duty it is to pass upon the quality of the steel that enters into the ingot that makes the sjjell. I have no complaint to make in regard to the inspectoral duties carried on by these experts. Their duties are very technical; and have to do with the analysis of the quality of the steel. In that respect a careful inspection has to be carried out, but when it comes to measuring the shells when they come from the presses-why, who are the men employed as inspectors? There is one political heeler from Cape Breton; there is another who had been engaged as a party scribbler in the Conservative press, a man who is known by every Liberal in my own constituency. And so it is down the whole list; that class of inspection is entirely under the control of the gentleman who has the patronage in my county. Hon. gentlemen need not come here and make any statements with regard to there being no politics in the matter, because these are the facts so far as my county is concerned, facts that cannot be questioned.
I am not going further into the question of the creation of this committee. I assume that the Government will bring down all the information that they have in their power to give in regard to that, that is, all the information which relates to the expenditures that have been made, all the information that they can bring down having regard to the limitations placed upon such questions in time of war. I wish to reiterate in the
	.

strongest and most emphatic way that so far as any evidence is before us at this moment, my hon. friend the Solicitor General has no warrant for the statement, either as a matter of law or as a matter of parliamentary practice, to say that the right of investigation is not in this Parliament. If my hon. friend the Solicitor General or any other -hon. member of this Government, came into this Parliament and said: Yes, we believe that this Shell Committee is a body which has done that which is honest and right, and, while it may have made mistakes, still, it is not entitled to be criticised; if any minister of the Crown ventured to take that position in regard to it and was able to satisfy Parliament and the people that that was a tenable position, that would be one thing; but when the Solicitor General and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries say: We will neither defend nor will we excuse, nor will we say that we yield any principles to this institution which we have divorced ourselves from and attached to the Imperial authorities in some imaginary way; we think it may have been wrong and that it ought to be investigated and all that, but the Imperial authorities, or some other people, are to do it-if, I say) they take that position, and if they expect from this House, and from Canada a continuation of those ideals Which many of us entertain in regard to this war, it. is an impossible position, a position liiey cannot take in the face of Canada and of this Parliament in regard to this question and they must realise it.
My hon. friend from North Essex (Mr. Wilcox) was put up the other day to deal with this question and to answer it. I want to say what one of their own papers said about that. We will leave out the Toronto Telegram. There is no use of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries coming to us and stating what the Free Press said, and thereby settling the whole question. Why do not these hon. gentlemen tell us something themselves, something that they know about, instead of taking the Free Press and saying that 'excuses the whole thing. What does the Free Press know about making shells? What has it had to do with the shell business? If it knows all about this thing, the Minister of Militia ought to attach the editor of the Free Press to his staff and put him in charge of the business of making shells. The ,minr isters themselves do not appear to know anything about it; they run away from the situation and say we will not stand up for the Shell Committee, and abuse my hon.

friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). This is *what the editor of the Montreal Evening News says with reference to the extraordinary remark which my hon. friend from North Essex made in the House the other day:
General Bertram and his associates may well cry to be saved from their friends.
There should be no stirring up of strife over a few old horses and a few shells.'
The remark was made seriously and will be taken seriously. . .
In the face of the evident unwillingness of the members of the Dominion Shell Committee to defend their honour, the country must look after its own honour which is also compromised in the charges that have been made. . . . The apologists of General Bertram must be told that they are doing a great disservice to that gentleman and his colleagues, to themselves, and to the country by their ostrich-like policy. As for the remark of the member for North Essex, it condemns itself. It is indeed beneath contempt.
I 'have attempted to emphasize as strongly as I could the duty which this Government *owes to the country and to Parliament of endeavouring, first, by the abolition, .and if not the abolition, the restriction at least, of patronage during the war, and by the taking of an attitude having a semblance of justice .and fairness in regard to the situation which has been created with reference to the Shell Committee, to put themselves in such a position that they can hold up to the 250,000 Canadian boys who will rally round the flag that ideal and those sentiments which they must have if they are going to come forward to fight for their country.
But there is .another thing that I think this Government should do in this regard having reference to the sentiments of the Canadian people. I am sorry that the hon. the Secretswy of State ((Hon. Mr. BlondSn) is not in the House. There is a certain duty that these hon. gentlemen who are his colleagues are charged with and one which they will not perform in regard to him. We all knew the constitutional principle of the collective responsibility of the members of the Government in regard to their views upon important questions. That is laid down by all the constitutional writers. I am speaking from the seat of a colleague admired and esteemed on both sides of this House, who is now in a German prison in Berlin because he was taken in Antwerp engaged in the humane task of giving succour by his medical science to Belgian wounded. Speaking by his authority, and repeating what he said to me, I want to say that there sits in this chamber in this time of stress when the heart of the nation is
stirred, a man who in 1910 on a platform in the province of Quebec, in the presence of Dr. Beland, fell on his knees on the platform and with hands uplifted in the attitude of prayer besought the Holy Virgin and all tbe( saints that the young men of the province of Quebec might be saved from the awful calamity that would come upon them if this Laurier naval law went into effect and they were asked to go and fight the battles of Great Britain upon the sea and be compelled to lose their lives on the deck of a British battleship. I am aware that the former Minister of Inland Revenue, now Secretary of State, has a habit of denying these things. But there is. something more that he said from his place in this Parliament in 1910. I find by reference to Hansard, page 44-53, 1910, that he said this:
I feel that I am bound to protest loudly against the policy of the Government and against that of my own party as regards the question of creating a Canadian Imperial war fleet or of making a cash contribution.
He loudly made that protest in Parliament, those of us who were here heard him, and you will find the statement in Hansard. In these days when all our hearts are stirred, when our boys are going out to fight, when the bodies of some of our friends are being left in Flanders and the Dardanelles, are we to have in this Government a man who has made this statement, which I have repeated here, and who has never taken it back as he should have taken it back right in this House. It will not do for this gentleman, with his last hour repentance, to make recruiting speeches in which he never disavows a single one of these utterances. What ideals will the boys of this land have in regard to governmental management when you find within its leadership a man who has never taken back these words and who will not now stand up in Parliament and declare that he has abandoned forever his nationalistic principles as he should do. I declare that this is a time for the searching of hearts upon questions of this kind, and it is up to the Secretary of State to let us know whether these recruiting meetings of his are wholly mockeries or whether he has foregone those sentiments which he reiterated all over Quebec.
Now let us take another honourable gentleman. We have not got to know him very well yet. He, (the Hon. Mr. Patenaude) is the successor of the former Minister of Inland Revenue now the Secretary of State. Mr. Bourassa declared, I am told, in Le Devoir that he was one of his great friends at St. Remi and other places in Quebec and



it is interesting to know what he thinks of the attitude of the Canadian people in war time. The Hon. Mr. Taschereau, whom, honourable gentlemen will recall, is the Minister in the province of Quebec who had a verbial encounter with Mr. Armand Lavergne, a week or so ago, spoke in the city of Toronto in the year 1909. Loyal and true Canadian, and lover of Britain he is, then as now entertaining sentiments to which we would all give adhesion. Mr. Taschereau, expressing his views said:
We consider that Canada develops in a marvellous manner; we feel that she is on the highway to nationhood; we recognize her as a part of the greatest Empire that ever existed: we think that Canada should hear her share of the burden that falls to the lot of all prosperous and growing countries; we believe that, for a long time to come, our future is bound up in the advancement and integrity of the Empire; we believe that a call coming from the Mother Country should be heard.
Will our sons serve on that fleet? In answer to that question I will cite the following fact: In one of our public squares, some years ago, a monument was erected in honour of eleven of our brightest youths of Quebec who had given their lives in South Africa. There were one thousand of them to go forth ; those who fell sleep under the sands of the dark continent, but their memories live in bronze to remind our children of the courage and loyalty of the Quebecers.
Gentlemen, what Quebec did in the past she will do again in the future, and when the trumpet calls, in true Canadian style, we will answer " present."
That is an extract from the speech of the Hon. Mr. Taschereau delivered in Toronto in December, 1909. In the following session of the Legislature, this motion was proposed by Mr. Pr&vost:
Whereas in December last, during a trip to Toronto, which the speech from the Throne has invested with an official character, the Minister of Public Works and of Labour declared himself, in the name of the province of Quebec and in presence of the Prime Minister, to be in favour of Canada's participation in the wars of the Empire, the formation of a Canadian war navy or of any other measure which the Federal authorities might deem proper to adopt in that regard;
This House regrets that one of the ministers of the province should have, without any mandate, upon subject foreign to the jurisdiction of the Government whereof he is a member, and under circumstances that impart a significant meaning to his words, made indiscreet declarations which are calculated to place the views of the electors of this province in a false light.
This resolution was voted upon, and I have the division list in my hand. Amongst other names appear those of Mr. Armand Lavergne and Mr. Patenaude in very singular proximity.
Who is Mr. Patenaude?

He is the new
Minister of Inland Revenue. At this time when naturally our hearts call for unity in all things, these two gentlemen, if they have ceased to entertain those sentiments and feelings which they entertained in 1910, should come forward and in the light of day before this Parliament and this country declare that such is the case, so that the boys who have gone out to fight and perhaps to die, may know that the men who compose the Government of this country are in earnest in ^regard to this question and are not fooling with them.
When was the Minister of Inland Revenue sworn in?

Some time last fall, I think. The remarks which I have made with regard to these gentlemen have not been made with any personal feeling, but under a deep sense of the serious attitude which I entertain towards this war and its consequences. There are hundreds of men in this country who entertain the same sentiments that I do; in fact, every one does who knows of these things, and I ask the Government under the circumstances to see to it that these men declare where they stand in this year of grace 1916, in view of the situation in which this country and the Empire now stand owing to the war.
We had this afternoon from my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) a lengthy and interesting speech in which he dealt with a variety of subjects. In regard to one or two of the matters to which he referred 9 p.m. I think he claimed a little too much credit. In the province from which I come, the lumber trade had last year reached the highest possible point. My hon. friend rather indicated that he was entitled to some especial credit by reason of the fact that in July, 1915, the Naval Service had taken some steps to arrange for vessels to carry lumber and other products to Great Britain, and the figures which he gave to the House were to the effect that more lumber had gone from our Maritime ports in the year 1915 than in either of the two immediately preceding years. That is true, and I am very glad to know that the hon. minister has made those arrangements in regard to the carrying of lumber. I am not quarrelling with him on that score; but from business dealings with clients and others connected with the lumber business, I know that in so far as that business in our part of the

Maritime Provinces is concerned, the arrangements for the sale of the lumber and for the carrying of it by Norwegian vessels were all made in the winter of 1914-15. Yet my hon. friend, if I understood him correctly, did not begin to make any arrangements until July, 1915. Therefore, while I am perfectly willing to give the minister all credit for any efforts put forth by him to encourage the transportation of our products to Great Britain, in that respect I think he is not entitled to the credit which he claims.
We hear from many sources that the ministry is overburdened with work. The stress of this war upon these hon. gentlemen is so great that they have to appoint commissions to do this, that and the other thing. Let us be perfectly frank about this matter. I recognize fully that the right hon. the Prime Minister of this country has at this critical time in our history, a very great and serious burden placed upon his shoulders, one which is probably the most onerous that any man in this country has ever had to bear. I make the same statement with regard to the gentleman who fills the position of Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes), and also with regard to the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). These three gentlemen have very serious and responsible duties to perform; but when I am told that my genial friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) has worked harder at his duties since the war began, I am asked to believe too much, because I fail to see where in the slightest degree this war has added to my hon. friend's burdens. We are told that only large public works are going on, and that the thousand and one details, that I have no doubt troubled the minister in the past, are absent. I see, however, that the expenditure is still maintained at a great height, and I wonder whether my hon. friend is really as busy in connection with this war as he is alleged to be. I believe that if we are able thoroughly to appreciate the situation, we shall find that the Minister of Public Works has very little to do in connection with -war matters. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) has so little to do at the present time that he is running not only his own department but the Department of Railways as well, and the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) is taking the time for a jaunt across the ocean to see his sons. That is a very laudable thing to do, and I have no complaint to make with regard to it, except 15 J
that I wish to look perhaps a little frankly at the situation and see how much there is in this mystery about the burden of care that is weighing these hon gentlemen down, with the exception of the first three whom I have mentioned.
Take the Minister of Inland Revenue to whom I referred a moment ago. How much is he worrying about the war? Or the Secretary of State (Mr. Blondin), how much is he worrying about it? Then there is the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche), he is having no immigrants to look after, and not many homesteads are being taken up. He is not working as hard as he used to. And the Postmaster General (Mr. Cas-grain) is not looking as if he were worrying about things. He goes about spending a good deal more money than his predecessors spent and adding a great number of people to the service, and though he has taken a large amount of money from the people he manages to acquire a deficit, which deficit is not due to the war in the slightest degree. The statement that it is due to the war will not hear analysis. So,
I go through the list of these gentlemen and I find that when one of their supporters talks about the awful burdens resting upon them, I wonder at the imagination of those who can believe it.
Take my hon. and genial friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and of the Naval Service (Mr. Hazen), he has been leaving undone the things he ought to have done' ever since the war began. He has not been attending' to his business at all. Let me show you in what respect he has failed. Take the Island of Newfoundland, the smallest of the British Dominions, with a population of a little over two hundred thousand, or about half that of the province of Nova Scotia. In addition to sending its quota of men to fight in the field, Newfoundland has sent a thousand men as naval brigade to fight upon the seas. Take Australia and New Zealand; three thousand of their Iboys have gone out as part of the naval service and have done marvellous work in the peninsula at Gallipoli. Then there is South Africa-South Africa with whom we were fighting only a short time ago. Why, Cape Colony sent to the naval brigade a first instalment of 1,692 men and has been sending reinforcements ever since. All these other oversea dominions have been there with naval assistance but, though we enjoy as they do the protection of the British navy, we have not done a single thing; the Minister of the Naval Service

has not even tried to do anything since this war began.
And, mark you, the need has been very great. Let me read to you an advertisement that appeared in the British papers. People talk about the necessity of having trained sailors, trained mechanics, in order to be of assistance in the naval brigade. But here is the advertisement-
Royal Naval Division-Public School Battalion.
The Admiralty have given official permission for raising a battalion of 1,000 men, which will be strictly limited to public school or university men and who will serve together as a unit.
Training is now going forward.
Applicants desiring to enrol should apply at once to
Royal Naval Division,
,	6, 7, 8, Old Bond Street, London, W.
Here is what they said last week in the Imperial House of Commons when this question was before them. An amendment was adopted to the Bill in regard to compulsory service by which the Admiralty was given first call on men desirous of enlisting in the navy. And the First Lord of Admiralty stated that a supplementary estimate would be presented for the expense of 50,000 men for the navy by next March. And here is what Mr. Ash-meade Bartlett, the brilliant war correspondent of whom we all have read, says, in regard to the naval conditions in the Dardanelles:
Mr. Ashmead Bartlett states that in some of the vessels off the Dardanelles there is hardly an active service rating on the upper deck. "There are many men between 48 and 56 years of age; nearly all are fathers and many are grandfathers. They have reached .hat age when, after a hard life at sea, they might reasonably expect to look forward to passing their declining years surrounded by their children and grandchildren, in the happy enjoyment of their small pensions, and engaged in the civilian pursuit each may have adopted at the conclusion of his period of active service."
That means simply that the condition is so serious that these men who had passed through all the stages of active service and had gone home have to be called out again in order to fill up the positions in the navy. We talk about having done our duty. Think of our tremendous sea-coast, stretching on the Atlantic from the Maine border around the province of New Brunswick, from which my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) comes, around what is almost an island, the province of Nova Scotia, then on the eastern side of New Brunswick away up the Baie des Cha-leurs and around the peninsula of Gaspe and all through that tremendous St. Lawrence territory; and then our British Col-

umbia coast running from Puget Sound up to Alaska. Can any man say that we are doing our duty when not one sailor boy has gone from Canada to assist the navy in this time of stress? South Africa has put us to shame. See what General Botha, who was fighting the Empire in 1900, said when the South African naval contingent started on its voyage to the scene of hostilities, where it has done such splendid service:
" Please convey to the commander, officers, and men of the Naval Contingent, South African Division of the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve, my warmest good wishes on their departure. It gives me and my government great pleasure to think that the Admiralty, by asking for their services, has recognized the good work and efficiency of the only naval unit which South Africa has yet been able to organize for the common cause. I feel confident that all ranks of the contingent, by constant devotion to duty and by irreproachable conduct, at all times, will show that South Africans, even though few in numbers, are worthy to he represented in that great naval service which is the pride and bulwark of the Empire, and now striving, as ever, to guard our most precious inheritance of justice and liberty."
And we have not got a man there at all. This is what Dr. Macnamara said in regard to the South African naval contingent:
Dr. Macnamara, in reply to a question by Commander Bellairs, states that the offer of the services of a number of the South African Royal Naval Vo'unteer Reserve was gladly accepted by the Admiralty, and the men are now attached to the Royal Naval Division in this country. It was understood that they wished to serve as a unit representing their corps. -
Now, there is this to be said about the Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes), that he has been energetic. Whatever criticism may be directed against his actions, and whether he has done right or wrong, a point which I am not considering at this moment, he has been busy; he has been " on to his job. " But the Minister of the Naval Service has not done anything, nor has he tried to do anything.
I have information to the effect that in 1912 a number of enthusiastic young men in Victoria, B.C., and surrounding districts, conceived the idea of forming a volunteer naval reserve similar to the one recruited in South Africa.
I am instructed that although that reserve was formed in 1912, they were unable to obtain any recognition from the Department of Naval Service until after the war began.
I have looked through the reports-I have them under my .hand-and I can find in them no mention of the Royal Volunteer reserve until, in the report of last year,

Admiral Kingsmill referred to the fact that such a body was in existence. Gentlemen from British Columbia will know whether or not what I say is correct. I am told that Sir Richard McBride, who was in England after the war began, wanted to raise a naval brigade in British Columbia; that this Government was approached in connection with the matter, and that-I am simply stating the information that comes to me from what I consider to be authentic sources; if I am not correct, hon. gentlemen will tell me-nothing was done either to encourage or to assist the project. In January and March, 1915, after that volunteer naval reserve had been formed, an order was issued notifying the men who had come together in that body that they had permission to retire from that service and to join the army instead of the navy. If these are the facts, I should like to Know from this Government why that condition of affairs has been allowed to exist. Shall we say that we are going to do nothing for the Empire upon the sea? Shall we say that we will not try to do anything? If so, the Newfoundland boys had better not have gone, the Cape Colony boys had better have stayed at home; and so with the boys from Australia. I am not going to renew the old discussion of naval matters; 1 am going to deal with this matter simpiy and solely from the standpoint of whether or noi we should be doing something upon the saa to aid Great Britain. I say that we should.
Hon. gentlemen tell us that this war was foreseen; that we should have done this, that or the other thing. But it was a strange thing if anybody in connection with the Naval Department foresaw the war. Here is the official report of 1914 in regard to the recruiting of men for the Canadian ships:
No recruits have been entered since 1st October, 1912, pending a decision being arrived at as to the future naval policy. The repairs to the Niobe were completed in December, and trials were carried out, which proved satisfactory ; the ship is now in an efficient seagoing condition, but is not able to undertake cruises, owing to a deficient complement, the active service ratings having been sent back to England without being replaced.
Which means that all men who could engage in active service on the Niobe in that year had been sent back to England, and nobody had been supplied to take their places. The same thing occurred in regard to the Rainbow. The report says:
The Rainbow made various cruises on the coast of Vancouver island until August, 1912, when the active service ratings were sent to
England and were not replaced, since when the ship has remained at Esquimalt, with occasional cruises to keep engines in an efficient condition.
That is the way things stood in 1912; let us see what where they were in the next year. The report says:
The Government having decided not to continue H.M.C. ships Niobe and Rainbow in full commission, no recruiting was carried on during the year, and the programme of exercises and training laid down for these ships was not continued. During the year free discharge was given to those Canadians who entered the service as boys and wished to avail themselves of the offer; in addition, many of the ranks and ratings lent from the Imperial service have completed their engagement .under the Canadian Government, and returned to England, without being replaced.
That was the situation in April, 1914, just before the war broke out. Having read this report, I say to hon. gentlemen that if they had any prescience of the war, they were dealing with it in a very strange way.
In September, 1915-that is, last year- we find mention for the first time of the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve. The report says:
The R.N.C.V.R., chiefly recruited at Esquimalt, have been actively and usefully employed both ashore and afloat, and have shown, both officers and men, commendable zeal in the performance of their duties.
That, mark you, was the first time we ever heard anything about a volunteer reserve of any kind. When the war broke out-it is told here in the books, and needs no amplification-the Niobe was tied up at the wharf, with not a man on board but the few officers who made their homes there. No recruiting had been done. While the Niobe was tied up at the wharf the valuable German vessel Willehad left Quebec, came down around the coast of Nova Scotia, passed the harbour of Halifax, and reached the port of Boston in absolute safety. According to these books, the Rainbow was in exactly the same position as the Niobe, and we were indebted to Japan *-Japan, mind you-for the protection of our western coast during a period of time after the beginning of the war and until the Newcastle came. It is just as well that our people should know the facts in connection with these matters. As soon as possible after the war, but too late to catch the German vessels now interned in New York and Boston, Great Britain sent out ships. The Niobe could have captured these German vessels; every naval officer will tell you that; they told me in Halifax that they, could have captured these ships

had the Niobe been afloat and ready for operation. About a month after that the Niobe came out. What for? To intercept *any German ships that might be in the vicinity of the coast. These were soon cleaned off the seas by Craddock and Stur-dee-and what are our ships doing now? What have they been doing all summer? It is the humiliating fact that the flagship of the squadron, which was off our coast last summer, was the Sidney, which had been built and equipped by the overseas Dominion of Australia. That was the flagship which headed the fleet that was off our coast last summer, and which was there chiefly for the purpose of guarding the trade routes to and from United States ports. When our transports wanted to cross the ocean last summer were they consorted by British ships? Not at all. If it had not been for the vessel with which Mr. Jack Boss presented the Government, the Grilse, which had been fitted up as a torpedo-boat destroyer, and which escorted practically all, if not all, of the transports which went from Quebec there would have been no protection against German submarines in the vicinity of the Atlantic coast. The Government of Canada did absolutely nothing in that regard. The people in the Maritime Provinces, in Montreal, and elsewhere in the province of Quebec, last year heard a good deal about the danger from German submarines. German submarines had found their way to the Mediterranean; in order to operate at a long distance from home waters, all they had to do was obtain a base of supply for oil and provisions.
A vessel of a neutral nation, say from Norway or Sweden, could carry these supplies to some inaccessible spot. Any one who knows anything of the geography of our sea coast knows that, and men who are connected with naval matters were fully convinced that it was possible last year that German submarines could have made a base anywhere along the western coast of the old colony of Newfoundland, or on the northern portion of Cape Breton, or on the southern portion of Nova Scotia. There was no reason why submarines could not have come out and operated from a base in any of these districts. If they had done so what protection had Canada? Mark you, the larger vessels are not the protection which countries have against submarines. There has been a wonderful development in regard to naval construction as the result of this war. Look at the stories of the battles that have taken place
'Mr. Macdonald.]
in the North sea, where the destructiveness of the submarines has sent to the bottom vessel after vessel of the ironclads of Great Britain, which were unable to protect themselves against the silent and stealthy message of death that came from the nose of these submarines. The only way to protect a vessel against these submarines is by a torpedo boat destroyer or another submarine. The minister said nothing in regard to that. Why has not the minister gone to the Vickers-Maxim Company in Montreal or some other industry and kept them busy during this winter building some submarines for the protection of our coast? Great Britain took the submarines that came from the Vickers-Maxim shipyards across the sea, under their own power. We have not a single submarine in Canada to defend ourselves. Why has not the Minister of the Naval Service done something in this regard? It is quite natural that gentlemen who do not live near the sea-and I do not wish to be understood as speaking in an offensive way-should not be fully alive to this matter; but I would strongly impress on this House and on this country that, through this Department of the Naval Service, some steps should be taken to defend both the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts from submarine attacks, There is little danger of a large German ironclad getting out. One might pop out from the North sea and get around the north of Scotland, but it could be easily caught. But the submarine could come out undetected, have hier base on the iSt. Lawrence or Cabot strait, and from there send to the bottom our transports crossing the ocean, for all the protection that Canada has. Every one in the Maritime Provinces says that and knows that; I am not stating any fact that is not fully known. The minister should even now proceed to provide protection by the construction of submarines and of torpedo-boat destroyers, which can be built in Montreal or elsewhere. I do not wish to go into this old argument of what Canada can do and what it cannot do do. But we have done it. We have gone ahead by the enterprise of our own people in this way, and have built submarines, and they have sailed across the ocean and, as the hon. member for St. John said this afternoon, one of them has performed marvellous work and rendered splendid service in the sea of Marmora. Shall we do nothing on the sea for Great Britain? Will we not even protect ourselves? 1 say to my hon. friends from British Columbia, who, I be-

lieve, ace very much interested in this question, that I regard it as the bounden duty of every one to face this situation -and, if the facts are as I have stated, the situation is one which must be dealt with, and dealt with speedily. I am not able to understand why the minister has not dealt with this question. I visited the dockyard in Halifax two weeks ago or a little over, and I was astounded to find that at that moment there was only one vessel that was able to go to sea out of all the vessels around the dockyard belonging to the Canadian Government. That was on the 2nd of January. The Canada was in the marine slip at Dartmouth. Here were two vessels purchased in the United! States last summer for which large prices were paid. They were taken to Montreal and a very great amount spent upon repairs. Then they were brought down there, and the information given to me very freely in the dockyard was that the captain of one of these vessels absolutely refused to go to sea. That was the condition of affairs on the 2nd of January, 1916, with this war on. All the British vessels at that moment were down in the West Indies, there was not a single one within hundreds of miles of the Nova Scotia coast, except one vessel, a sort of lame duck, which was able to struggle out. There was quite a regiment of little tugs and other small boats which were of no use whatever. Again, here in this dockyard, built by the money of the Imperial Government, which the Imperial vessels use but very rarely and to a very slight extent, anybody who looks honest to the Dominion policeman who 'Stands at the gate of the dockyard can walk in and go anywhere he pleases. I say the Minister of the Naval Service should have that dockyard under the control of men who are there attached to the Niobe. There are seven or eight hundred men there on the Niobe, which was being dismantled, at least her guns were being taken off.
Mr. 'CARVELL: Again?

Again, the guns were being taken off her, she was practically being torn to pieces. I asked some of these seven ot eight hundred men what they were going to do and they said they did not know. There was nobody guarding the dockyard gate except a Dominion policeman. If this Naval Service is not the most awful farce that any Government ever intended to carry through in any country, do you not think that they would have some of their men detailed to
guard the gates of this dockyard at the city of Halifax, which is supposed to be the great centre of the Atlantic squadron on this side of the ocean? Yet that was the situation. It seems to me surprising,
I am bound to say I was astounded,
I bring this matter to the attention of [Parliament not from any desire to be partisan in placing the matter before the House; but I believe that these conditions axe such that Parliament should know of them, th< country should be informed of them, and the matter should be dealt with accordingly. What are we to do 'in regard to this matter? I should like to have any hon. member of the Government tell me why, with our magnificent Atlantic and Pacific sea coasts, we should not send over to England some men to help the fleet, to join the naval division, to take the places of those hardy old men who have been dragged from their homes to go out and fight at Gallipoli because the younger men could not be had. We have been doing splendidly in sending boys to fight on the land; but around the sea coast of this great Dominion there are as many men, just as good and stout hearts, who go down to the sea in ships, and . make their living amid the perils of the life of a fisherman, who would make .splendid material for the navy. There are many more of these men in Canada than there are in the colony of Newfoundland. Why aTe these boys not asked to go and join the Imperial fleet? I venture to say that in the county of Guysborough there axe hundreds of men who would be willing to go and who would acquit themselves nobly as the boys from Newfoundland have done. Will anybody say why they should not go? Among hon. gentlemen living in the interior of this country in our great inland centres, from Montreal to the Rocky mountains, it is quite natural that there should be apathy in this matter. I can quite appreciate the fact that the man who lives m Winnipeg or in Western Canada generally, who is away from the Great Lakes, would not know, as those of us who have lived on the seaboard from boyhood know, just what the possibilities are in that regard. I know there are boys in my county who would much rather go into the navy than into the army, but they have never been asked to go; no opportunity has been given to them to go. I am sure that that is true of the constituencies of hon. gentlemen on both sides of politics, and I would ask the minister to seriously consider the

matter, and let us have a statemient at some later period as to whether or not it would be possible to offer to Great Britain a naval brigade, and so do what South Africa, Newfoundland, New Zealand and Australia have done,
I would like to ask, too, in view of the tremendous amount of money which we are spending in connection with this war for all kinds of purposes, whether there is any reason why we should not have two torpedo boat destroyers on our Atlantic seaboard. We have the Grilse, a converted [DOT]steam yacht, but outside of the Grilse there is no boat that could catch or cope with a submarine if it happened to come through [DOT]the Straits of Belle Isle. Why should there not be destroyers in course of construction at Montreal which would be ready for the summer, and why should not the same condition exist in regard to the Pacific coast? I seriously urge upon my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that this is a problem which ought to be dealt with at once. In these matters we must look ahead, as well as at present conditions. The old theory that we could not build steel ships in Canada has been entirely exploded; there is no longer any room for argument in that respect.
What are the people of this country going to do when the war is over? Already you hear mutterings from our western friends in regard to the transportation of the great wheat crop, complaints as to freight rates, and as to the failure of the Government to get ships to carry the grain; and these conditions will continue, I warn the Government, until Canada sets herself to provide and equip herself properly for transportation upon the sea just as she has equipped herself so magnificently upon the land. To-day we have three transcontinental lines stretching from one end of this country to the other, and after the war is over we look for an immigration which will exceed anything we have had before. Add 100,000,000 bushels of -grain every year to the production of western Canada, bring them down to our seaports, and then what are you going to do? Are you never going to build ships; are we never going to provide for transportation on the sea just the same as on the land? I say, Sir, that this is the time for the examination of the conditions of the future. Unless the Government at this juncture immediately proceeds to give special encouragement to transportation so that we may have a merchant marine upon the seas, those who live inland may be 
pardoned if, with their inexact knowledge of marine matters, they think probably that their business will be paralysed. When this terrible war is over, we must look forward to a readjustment of conditions. Mr Speaker, I have already talked too long
Go on.

I hope that the imperfect remarks I have made will not be misunderstood. I have spoken strongly on some questions, but I have refrained from approaching the consideration of those problems, in so far as it is possible to do so, in the spirit of keen or aggressive partisanship.
An hon. MEMBER Oh, oh.

My hon. friend who wears the uniform ought to be earning the money for it and should refrain from sniggering. When hon. gentlemen like my hon. friend from Lunenburg come into this House as majors of medical corps, I am bound to say that I do not understand why, if they are on active service, they are not attending to their medical duties instead of coming here, or how their medical duties are performed in their absence. They should either do the one thing or the other. There are certain hon. gentlemen whose imputations I might not resent, but I do resent any such imputation as that thrown upon me by my hon. friend when he suggests that I have approached these questions upon a partisan plane. I have endeavoured in all sincerity to approach them on a higher ground than ordinarily. The views I have presented in regard to this whole matter have reference to questions which the people of this country and the Government ought to seriously consider at this juncture. I am sincerely desirous that at this stage in dur country's history we should endeavour in Parliament to hold up an example to the boys who have gone and who are going to the front, and that when we go to recruiting meetings and ask our young men to make sacrifices in order that our liberties may be maintained, we should show them an example and convince them that we know what we are talking about. We must correct the mistakes of the past and of the present as we go along; that is what Parliament is here for, that is our duty as representatives of a free people. Not only that; we should look forward to the future. Moreover, our duty to-day is not only in regard to these material things. Let us remember what was said at the time of the American war. Let us strive to finish

the work we are in and to bind up the nation's wounds, and let us do the best we can for the widows and the children of those who are fighting for Canada and the Empire.
The question of pensions, which was discussed this afternoon by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, is one of great importance, and one which I was delighted to see my hon. friend approach in the manner he did, because I regard it as one of the most important matters which could be considered by the members of this House. Hon. gentlemen will probably remember that a gentleman in Toronto, Mr. Frank Darling, prepared a pamphlet which discussed the question of pensions in a most interesting way. After that pamphlet had been brought to my attention, I placed on the order paper a notice of motion in regard to this matter, so that the whole question may come up for discussion at a later day. However, i appreciate very much indeed the action of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in placing upon Hansard' the information which he gave us this afternoon, because it is a question in which hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, no matter what their political predilections may be, are interested, and one with which they are anxious to deal fairly.
Over and above that, there is a question which has not, perhaps, been specially mentioned. One of the great problems, apart from pensions, is, what is to be done with the soldier who comes back partly injured and entitled to receive a pension, but who desires to avoid living a life of idleness. I understand that the Government have appointed a commission to deal with that question, with Senator Lougheed as chairman, but I wish to suggest, as I am interested in that question, having taken it up in Nova Scotia, that that committee is too large. The matter should be taken hold of by a minister, and dealt with by him on his responsibility as a minister. The relations between the Federal Governemnt and the Provincial Governments are very close and intimate in regard to this matter, and require attention in a greater degree than can be given by a commission. Provincial committees have been appointed also to deal with this matter. Complaints have been made as to the difficulty of getting together and working out these problems. I want to make a suggestion with all deference to the gentlemen who compose that commission, and I do so without making any reflection upon
them, but living as they do, in various portions of the country and being engaged in various occupations, it is almost impossible for them to get together and have that concentration and community of ideas which is necessary in order to work out that problem. It is becoming more acute every day. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) referred to cases that have come under his observation. There are young men who have come back to our part of the country and they are in the same way. While drawing their pensions, their future should be anticipated. Then, there comes in the problem of the development of technical education. By careful consideration of the possibilities of technical schools you may be able to give all these veterans that species of education which would enable them to fit themselves for earning an honest livelihood for themselves and their children, in addition to receiving their pensions. Then, there would be the avoidance of those conditions which we have heard from story and history, are always to be found after a war-the lack of employment and the lack of interest in the men who have fought for the nation. That has occurred in the Old Land, and history always repeats itself. My suggestion in regard to that question would be that some one of the ministers should take that matter under his direct control with his own staff and deal with it, and be the means of communicating directly between this Government and the various Provincial Governments whose assistance and cooperation may be desired.
The problems of the future for Canada are very serious. Already they are engaging the attention of out press. I see that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) has made an address upon this question and has been looking to the future in that regard. How these things will shape themselves is a. matter which is most difficult, no matter how far seeing any one may be, to tell with any degree of certainty. This much we do know, however, that there ought to be coming to this land from the older countries an immigration of even greater extent than that which came in the past. There ought to be special attention paid by the Government to this problem.
Again let me say that I have no faith in these commissions that this Government persist in appointing. The British system in relation to constitutional government is that the members of the Administration of the day, on account of their having been

trained in public affairs, and with that sense of responsibility which is always possessed by men in public life to a greater degree than those who have not had the experience, with that intimate knowledge of the conditions of Government that only men on the treasury benches can have, are the proper ones to deal with these questions, and, if they have the ability to do it, they should be seized of their responsibility and should endeavour to formulate and lay down whatever plans they can conceive for the future. Whatever our notion may be about the position of this 'Government in that regard is one thing, but this duty is one which ought to be seized by the Government themselves. If there is any device, any method by which attention can be properly directed to Canada when the day of victory comes, this plan ought to be thought out and developed by a responsible minister who would have the advantage of being able to provide in advance in their executive administration for the conditions which would produce the desired result.
It has occurred to me that a suggestion might be made in that regard as to how to deal with a condition that has 'been found a difficulty in the past. We find it in our province and I am sure it exists elsewhere. Take the .small farmer in a European country and bring him out and put him on a farm in the East or the West; he buys a farm in the least of 100 or loO acres and if he goes west he gets a homestead of 160 acres. Both of these farms are entirely too big for him, they are beyond anything he ever had to do with before and the consequence is that he is endeavouring to deal with a problem so far beyond anything he has ever attempted in his own country that he gives up after a short time and drifts into the city. You should endeavour to provide him with a homestead, or to put him in possession of a holding, smaller in area and under conditions more in consonance with those of the country from which he came and more in keeping with the conditions that exist where he grew up. In that way you would have a collection or a colony of people who, living together, would have a community of interest and you would dtevelop all those (conditions that go to make happy homes and to make life interesting. That is a problem, however, which I am quite sure hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House who know the West better than I do are more able to deal with

than I am. I only throw out that suggestion because it appears to me to be one that is well worthy of consideration.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have spoken very much longer than I had intended. In this third war session, with a deeper appreciation throughout the country and in the hearts and minds of every one of us as to the position in which we are at this time, I think that, in so far as it is possible for us to do so, we should endeavour to proceed to our duties with the understanding that the interests of Canada shall be advanced first and last, and that if possible division and dissension may be avoided upon non-essential matters. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have no right to complain, and must not complain, if there have been errors in the administration, if there have been mistakes which are injurious to the commonwealth, if we, in pursuance of our duties, as members of Parliament, point them out. If investigations should be had they should be granted at this time more than any other time. We owe this duty not only to ourselves, but to the people, who are watching to see how the affairs of Canada are being carried on.
As yet there are very few signs of the beginning of the end. There have been many dark days in the year and a half since this war began, but every one who has studied the story of the great nation to which we belong remembers that all down through the stormy pages of the history of the islands where to-day and for so many years has been foupd the centre of this Empire, there have been times when things looked far darker than they do today. Recall the days of the Crimea; the older men who lived in that period told you of the sad hearts in England, and of the doubts and fears which existed there as to whether or not the issue of the war would be favourable. Following that were the days of the Mutiny, of horrible atrocities in India with the great nation in tliat southern land which had always been associated with Great Britain in revolt against the Mother Country, and under conditions which indicated that that revolt very likely would be permanent. These days of gloom passed by. So will, I feel sure, these days of doubt and uncertainty; they will be dissipated, and if we Canadians, as true believers in that constitutional government which we have inherited from our fathers, will do our duty so that we may transmit to our children those principles of freedom

and justice which have come to us, we will be fulfilling in some measure our ideals, and will be laying the foundation of that future prosperity and greatness which I hope and believe we in Canada will see with certainty.
